topic: Introduction to Health Insurance and the Health System in India
t: The first structured hospitalisation insurance product sold to the general public in India, introduced in 1986 by the public sector general insurers, was known as:
e: Mediclaim (1986) was the first standard hospitalisation cover for individuals; Jan Arogya (1996), Bhavishya Arogya (1990) and UHIS (2003) came later.

topic: Introduction to Health Insurance and the Health System in India
t: The first stand-alone health insurance company to be registered in India was:
e: Star Health was registered in 2006 as the first stand-alone health insurer; Apollo DKV (later Apollo Munich) followed in 2007 and Max Bupa in 2008.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: The Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY), launched in 2008, offered BPL families a hospitalisation cover of:
o: ₹30,000 per family per year on a floater basis
e: RSBY provided ₹30,000 per family of five with a ₹30 registration fee and a smart card; it was subsumed by PM-JAY, which offers ₹5 lakh.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: The Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) is best described as:
o: A commercial health insurance product sold by public sector insurers
A contributory scheme providing comprehensive health care to central government employees, pensioners and their dependants in specified cities
A State-run scheme for below-poverty-line families
A reinsurance scheme for government employees' claims
e: CGHS, started in 1954, is a government-managed scheme funded by contributions and budget, not an insurance product; it operates in listed cities.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Community-based health insurance schemes such as those run by cooperatives or NGOs in India are generally characterised by:
o: Voluntary membership, small premiums and local pooling among members of a defined community
Pricing based on individual medical underwriting
e: CBHI schemes (e.g. Yeshasvini for cooperative farmers) rely on voluntary enrolment and local solidarity with low flat premiums; they are not individually underwritten.

t: A 'top-up' health policy (as distinct from a super top-up) pays:
o: Only when a single hospitalisation claim exceeds the deductible
When the aggregate of all claims in a year exceeds the deductible
e: A plain top-up applies the deductible per claim, so smaller multiple claims never trigger it; a super top-up applies the deductible to total claims in the policy year.

t: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the Arogya Sanjeevani standard product?
o: Cumulative bonus of 5% per claim-free year up to 50%
Unlimited room rent without any cap
Cataract sub-limit of 25% of sum insured or ₹40,000 per eye, whichever is lower
e: Arogya Sanjeevani caps room rent at 2% of sum insured (max ₹5,000 per day) and ICU at 5%; the other three features are part of the standard wording.

t: Under the 2024 Master Circular on health insurance, an insurer must decide on a cashless pre-authorisation request within:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Cashless authorisation must be decided within 1 hour of the request and final discharge authorisation within 3 hours; delay beyond 3 hours makes any extra hospital charges the insurer's cost.

t: A 'group health insurance' policy is issued to:
o: Any set of individuals who approach the insurer together to obtain a discount
A group that exists for a purpose other than obtaining insurance, such as employer-employee or members of an association
e: IRDAI permits group cover only for groups with a commonality of purpose other than insurance; a group formed merely to buy insurance is not eligible.

t: Mr Khan's policy of ₹10 lakh carries a 20% co-payment for insureds above 60 years. He is 62 and his admissible hospital bill is ₹2,40,000. The amount the insurer will pay is:
e: Co-pay of 20% means the insured bears ₹48,000 and the insurer pays 80% × ₹2,40,000 = ₹1,92,000.

t: The Corona Kavach policy introduced in 2020 was:
o: A benefit-based policy paying a lump sum on COVID-19 diagnosis
An indemnity-based standard policy covering hospitalisation for COVID-19, including home care
e: Corona Kavach was the indemnity standard product (including home care treatment), whereas Corona Rakshak paid a lump-sum benefit on positive diagnosis with 72 hours' hospitalisation.

t: An overseas travel medical insurance policy typically differs from a domestic health policy in that it:
o: Can be bought only after arriving abroad
Provides emergency medical expenses abroad in foreign currency, often with assistance services and travel-related covers
e: Travel medical cover is for emergencies during the trip, usually denominated in USD/EUR with assistance companies and add-ons like baggage loss; pre-existing conditions are generally excluded.

t: Which statement about a hospital daily cash product is correct?
o: The benefit is reduced proportionately if the actual room rent is lower
It can be claimed in addition to an indemnity policy for the same hospitalisation
The insured must submit original hospital bills for reimbursement of expenses
It cannot be bought by a person who already has mediclaim
e: Being a fixed-benefit product, hospital cash pays the agreed daily amount on proof of hospitalisation irrespective of expenses and can be claimed alongside an indemnity policy; original bills are not required.

t: The primary objective of health insurance underwriting is to:
o: Reject as many proposals as possible to keep claims low
Classify risks and charge premiums that match the risk so that the pool remains equitable and solvent
Sell the maximum number of policies
e: Underwriting aims at proper risk selection and classification, not rejection; this protects the pool from anti-selection while keeping products saleable.

t: Which of the following is generally the MOST important underwriting factor for individual health insurance?
o: Age and current medical history of the person to be insured
e: Age and medical history drive expected morbidity and claims; other factors such as occupation and lifestyle are secondary, and payment mode is not a risk factor.

t: A proposer discloses controlled hypertension for 5 years with no complications. The most likely underwriting response for a standard indemnity policy is:
o: Accept at standard rates with no condition
Issue the policy only as a benefit policy
Accept with a loading and/or a waiting period for hypertension-related conditions
e: Well-controlled hypertension is an impaired but insurable risk; insurers typically apply a loading, PED waiting period or a specific exclusion rather than declining.

t: Which of the following statements about premium loading at renewal of an individual health policy is correct?
o: Insurers may load the premium of an individual policy based on that insured's own claims in the previous year
Loading at renewal is permitted up to 100% of premium
Loading at renewal based on an individual's claims experience is not permitted; revisions must apply to the product as a whole
Loading is permitted only for senior citizens
e: IRDAI norms prohibit individual claim-based loading at renewal; premium changes must be filed for the entire product so that claimants are not penalised selectively.

t: The underwriting principle that a proposer is bound to disclose all material facts, whether asked or not, flows from:
o: Principle of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei)
e: Utmost good faith obliges the proposer to disclose material facts such as prior illnesses; breach allows the insurer to avoid the contract within the moratorium period.

t: Mr Arora holds a base policy of ₹3 lakh and a super top-up of ₹10 lakh with an aggregate deductible of ₹3 lakh. In one year he has three hospitalisations costing ₹2 lakh, ₹1.5 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh. How much will the super top-up pay in total?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Total claims are ₹6 lakh; a super top-up applies the deductible to aggregate annual claims, so it pays ₹6 lakh − ₹3 lakh = ₹3 lakh. An ordinary top-up would have paid nothing because no single claim exceeded ₹3 lakh.

t: A 48-year-old proposer with a BMI of 36 and fasting blood sugar of 160 mg/dl applies for a ₹20 lakh policy. The underwriter is most likely to:
o: Treat the case as sub-standard and consider a loading, exclusion of diabetes-related complications or a lower sum insured
Accept at standard terms because the sum insured is high
Decline because the proposer is above 45 years
Accept only on a family floater basis
e: Class II obesity combined with elevated fasting sugar indicates likely diabetes and higher morbidity; such risks are rated sub-standard and handled through loading, exclusions or restricted cover.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: For the purpose of a standard health policy, 'hospitalisation' means admission in a hospital for a minimum period of:
e: The standard definition requires 24 consecutive in-patient hours, relaxed for listed day care procedures where technology permits shorter stays.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: The standard exclusion code 'Excl03' in IRDAI's standardised list refers to:
o: 30-day initial waiting period for all illnesses except accidents
e: Excl01 is PED, Excl02 is the specified disease waiting period and Excl03 is the 30-day waiting period, which does not apply to accidental hospitalisation.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Which of the following 'modern treatments' must be covered under health policies as per IRDAI's 2019 guidelines, subject to sub-limits if any?
e: The guidelines list twelve modern treatments including robotic surgery, oral chemotherapy, immunotherapy and stem cell therapy that cannot be excluded; wellness, supplements and overseas treatment remain excludable.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: An insured has two indemnity health policies of ₹3 lakh and ₹5 lakh from different insurers. A hospital bill of ₹2 lakh is admissible under both. Under current IRDAI norms the insured may:
o: Claim only from the insurer whose policy is older
Choose either insurer to settle the claim, and claim the balance from the other if the first policy's limit is exhausted
Claim only in proportion to the sums insured
e: IRDAI allows the policyholder to select the insurer; contribution in proportion applies only where the claim exceeds the chosen policy's sum insured and the balance is sought from the other.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: A policy has a sum insured of ₹5 lakh and a cumulative bonus of 10% for each claim-free year up to 50%. After three consecutive claim-free years, the sum insured available in the fourth year is:
e: Cumulative bonus accrues 10% of the base sum insured per claim-free year: 3 × ₹50,000 = ₹1.5 lakh, giving ₹6.5 lakh; the 50% cap (₹2.5 lakh) is not yet reached.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: The clause requiring an insured with more than one policy to disclose this and limiting recovery to the actual loss is based on the principle of:
e: Contribution prevents profit from multiple indemnity policies by sharing the loss among insurers; subrogation concerns recovery from third parties.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: The 'burning cost' method of pricing a group health policy involves:
o: Charging the same premium as the previous year irrespective of claims
Using the national average claim ratio
Dividing the group's actual claims over past years by exposure to derive a base rate, then adding loadings for inflation and expenses
Pricing on the basis of the employer's turnover
e: Burning cost uses the group's own historical claims per exposure unit as the starting point, adjusted for trend, IBNR and expense loadings; it is the standard method for large experience-rated groups.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: Medical inflation of 12% per year is expected. A procedure costing ₹1,00,000 today is expected to cost approximately how much after two years?
e: Compounding: ₹1,00,000 × 1.12 × 1.12 = ₹1,25,440; simple addition of 24% would understate the trend that actuaries build into pricing.

t: A health insurer has a 40% quota share treaty. On a policy with premium ₹20,000 and a claim of ₹1,50,000, the reinsurer's share of the claim is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Under quota share the reinsurer takes the agreed fixed percentage of every premium and claim: 40% × ₹1,50,000 = ₹60,000; the insurer retains ₹90,000.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: The Insurance Information Bureau of India (IIB) is important for health insurers because it:
o: Sets maximum premiums for health products
Pays claims on behalf of insurers
Maintains industry-wide claims and policy data that supports pricing, fraud detection and hospital benchmarking
e: IIB, promoted by IRDAI, collects transaction-level data from all insurers; TPA licensing and claim payment are not its functions.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: 'IBNER' differs from 'IBNR' in that IBNER refers to:
o: Claims not yet reported to the insurer
The expected development (increase or decrease) in the cost of claims that have already been reported but are not fully settled
Claims reported after the policy expiry
e: Incurred But Not Enough Reported captures inadequacy in case reserves of known claims, whereas IBNR covers claims not yet notified at all.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: A health insurer's combined ratio is 108%. This indicates that:
o: The insurer earned an underwriting profit of 8%
Claims and expenses together exceeded earned premium by 8%, i.e. an underwriting loss
e: Combined ratio = incurred claims ratio + expense ratio; above 100% means an underwriting loss which must be offset by investment income to remain profitable.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The statutory body that regulates health insurance in India was established under the:
e: IRDAI was constituted under the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999; the Insurance Act 1938 is the substantive law it administers.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under Section 41 of the Insurance Act, 1938, offering a rebate of premium as an inducement to buy a health policy is:
o: Prohibited and punishable with a penalty of up to ₹10 lakh
e: Section 41 bars rebating by any person; the 2015 amendment raised the penalty to up to ₹10 lakh.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under IRDAI's TPA regulations, a Third Party Administrator:
o: May reject health claims on its own authority
Provides health services such as cashless processing and claim servicing on behalf of the insurer, but cannot reject a claim
Underwrites the policy and fixes the premium
Is a reinsurer for health claims
e: TPAs are service providers; the decision to admit or reject a claim remains with the insurer, and TPAs do not underwrite or reinsure.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 requires that:
o: Mental illness be excluded from all health policies
Mental illness be covered only after a 4-year waiting period
Every insurer make provision for medical insurance for treatment of mental illness on the same basis as physical illness
Only government hospitals treat mental illness
e: Section 21(4) of the Act mandates parity of cover for mental illness, which IRDAI enforced through its circulars and the 2019 exclusion guidelines.

t: The permitted limit of foreign direct investment in an Indian insurance company is currently:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Raised from 49% to 74% by the Insurance (Amendment) Act 2021; intermediaries may have 100%.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Which of the following statements about portability of health insurance is correct?
o: Portability allows transfer of credit for waiting periods already served to a new insurer, on a similar product
Portability is available only between policies of the same insurer
The new insurer must accept the proposal irrespective of underwriting
Portability can be exercised at any time during the policy year
e: Portability carries forward waiting-period credit (and accrued continuity benefits) to a new insurer at renewal; the new insurer still underwrites the proposal. Switching products within the same insurer is 'migration'.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under the 2024 framework, the maximum waiting period an insurer may impose for pre-existing diseases in a health policy is:
e: IRDAI reduced the maximum PED waiting period from 48 to 36 months in 2024; the specified-disease waiting period is also capped at 36 months.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (as per pecuniary limits notified in December 2021), a District Commission can entertain a complaint against an insurer where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed:
e: The 2021 rules set the District Commission limit at ₹50 lakh, State Commission up to ₹2 crore and National Commission above ₹2 crore; the original 2019 Act had higher limits.

t: Under the 2024 Master Circular, when a hospital requests final authorisation at the time of discharge, the insurer must grant it within:
e: Final discharge authorisation must be given within 3 hours; if delayed, additional charges levied by the hospital are to be borne by the insurer from shareholders' funds.

t: The 'Bima Bharosa' portal operated by IRDAI is a:
o: Portal for buying standard health products
Integrated grievance management system through which policyholders can register and track complaints against insurers
e: Bima Bharosa (formerly IGMS) lets policyholders lodge grievances that are routed to the insurer's grievance cell and monitored by IRDAI.

t: In the context of service quality, a 'moment of truth' in health insurance is best illustrated by:
o: The actuary filing the product with IRDAI
The interaction when a hospitalised customer's cashless request is processed
e: Moments of truth are customer touchpoints that shape perception; claim and cashless interactions are the most critical in health insurance.

t: Under the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) Regulations 2024, the free-look period for a policy with a term of one year or more is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). 30 days from receipt of the policy document, irrespective of the sales channel.

t: 'Phantom billing' by a hospital refers to:
o: Billing for services or tests that were never actually provided
Charging a higher tariff for a procedure than performed
Splitting a package into separately billed components
Billing a patient under another person's policy
e: Phantom billing is charging for non-existent services; the other options describe upcoding, unbundling and impersonation respectively.

t: Which of the following is an example of 'soft' fraud by a policyholder?
o: Inflating a genuine claim by adding a few extra bills for non-related medicines
Staging a fake hospitalisation with forged bills
e: Soft fraud is opportunistic exaggeration of a genuine claim; staged events, fake hospitals and impersonation are planned 'hard' fraud.

t: An insurer notices that one agent's portfolio has a 30-day-waiting-period claim rate five times the company average, mostly from the same two hospitals. The most appropriate first step is:
o: Cancel all policies sold by the agent
Increase premiums for all customers in that city
Ignore it as a statistical variation
Use data analytics to flag the agent-hospital cluster for investigation and tighten pre-policy checks on that portfolio
e: Fraud frameworks call for analytics-driven identification of clusters and targeted investigation; blanket cancellation is unlawful without proof and city-wide loading is not permitted.

t: The obligatory cession that Indian general and health insurers must currently make to GIC Re on every policy is:
e: The obligatory cession was reduced from 5% to 4% with effect from 2022-23; it applies to each policy subject to specified limits.

t: A newly licensed stand-alone health insurer with limited capital and no claims history is most likely to protect its portfolio with:
o: A per-risk excess of loss cover with a very high retention
A catastrophe excess of loss cover only
No reinsurance, since health claims are small
A quota share treaty that shares premium and claims proportionally and provides capital relief
e: Quota share gives a new insurer solvency relief, reinsurer expertise and ceding commission; per-risk XL is less useful for high-frequency, low-severity health claims.

t: A health insurer buys an aggregate stop-loss treaty covering losses in excess of a 95% loss ratio up to 120%. Its net earned premium is ₹200 crore and net incurred claims are ₹220 crore. The reinsurer pays:
e: Actual loss ratio is 110%; the treaty responds from 95% to 120%, so the recovery is (110% − 95%) × ₹200 crore = ₹30 crore.
